Brabant
bra-BANT
n. (the central duchy of the Low Countries, where the Reformation's first martyrs died and whose university condemned Luther first)
Latin Brabantia, from the Frankish bracha, newly broken land, and bant, a district; the duchy held Brussels, Antwerp, Louvain and Bois-le-Duc.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Brabant is the duchy in which the Reformation was first condemned and first paid for in blood. Louvain, its university, was the earliest faculty in Europe to censure Luther, publishing its condemnation in November 1519 before Rome had finished its own process, and its theologians afterwards drew up the indexes of forbidden books for the Netherlands. Brussels, its chief residence, was where the Augustinians Hendrik Voes and Jan van Esch were burned on 1 July 1523, the first men executed anywhere for Reformation doctrine; their house at Antwerp was suppressed and its prior imprisoned. Antwerp itself, Brabant's port and for a generation the richest city in northern Europe, was the Low Countries' printing capital and its most mixed population, Lutheran, Calvinist, Anabaptist and Catholic at once, until the Spanish recapture of 1585 drove its Protestants north. Brabant was divided by the war: the north became Dutch and largely remained Catholic in population, the south stayed with Spain. The dictionary enters Brabant because the firsts belong here. The first censure, the first index, the first martyrs and the first great Protestant press were all in one duchy, and the Reformation's opponents moved faster in it than anywhere else.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an index as a table of contents or a list of prohibited books; to censure as to blame or condemn; a faculty as the body of professors; and a prior as the superior of a convent.

expand to see more

INDEX, n. A table of contents; among the Romanists, a catalogue of prohibited books.

CENSURE, v. To find fault with and condemn as wrong; to blame; to express disapprobation of.

FACULTY, n. The body of professors or masters in a university, or in one of its departments of learning.

PRIOR, n. The superior of a convent of monks, or one next in dignity to an abbot.

STAKE, n. A small piece of wood sharpened at one end; the post to which one condemned to be burnt was fastened.

Modern Corruption

Central duchy of the Low Countries, whose university at Louvain condemned Luther in 1519 and whose capital burned the first Reformation martyrs in 1523.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the index, the list of books a people may not read, of which Louvain's theologians were the Netherlands' principal authors. An index assumes what the Reformation denied, that the laity must be protected from the text by men who have it; and it is answered not by a counter-list but by the apostles' reply when they were forbidden to teach, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). Brabant's indexes were enforced with real severity, and Antwerp's printers went on working anyway.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the martyr's blessing is attached to the cause and not to the quantity. Two Augustinians died at Brussels in 1523, which is a small number beside the thousands who followed them, and the word over them is the same: “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10). They are the first of the company seen “under the altar” (Rev 6:9) in the Low Countries, and the dictionary notes that their own faculty at Louvain had supplied the sentence four years before the fire was lit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dioko (G1377), to persecute, to pursue; Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; Greek thusiasterion (G2379), an altar.

expand to see more

Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, to persecute; “Blessed are they which are persecuted”, Matthew 5:10.

Greek dikaiosune (G1343) — righteousness, equity; “persecuted for righteousness' sake”, Matthew 5:10.

Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; “We ought to obey God rather than men”, Acts 5:29.

Greek thusiasterion (G2379) — an altar, a place of sacrifice; “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain”, Revelation 6:9.

Greek prizo (G4249) — to saw asunder; “They were stoned, they were sawn asunder”, Hebrews 11:37.

Usage

"“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the Louvain indexes of forbidden books."

"“Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10) — Voes and Van Esch at Brussels, 1 July 1523."

"“I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain” (Rev 6:9) — a university's censure four years before the fire."
